posts.title: Painful arc: document the finding

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: a painful arc is a symptom pattern—not automatic proof of “impingement,” tissue pinching, or one damaged tendon.

Quick check: B. “Familiar pain from 70–110° during elevation” documents what you actually observed. Record onset and easing angles while raising and lowering the arm, plus the plane used. A midrange arc is commonly described around 60–120°, but the exact pattern belongs to the person in front of you.

A painful arc can modestly support a cuff-related pain hypothesis in context. Its absence does not settle the diagnosis. Save this before shoulder lab—and send it to the classmate who writes only “positive.”

posts.title: Hawkins-Kennedy: provoke, then describe

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: Hawkins-Kennedy is a symptom-provocation maneuver. A painful response does not identify one tendon, demonstrate tissue pinching, or establish a tear.

Quick check: B. In the taught setup, the examiner supports the arm and gradually guides passive internal rotation within tolerance; the patient is not performing a resisted force task. Record familiar pain, position limits, and any modification. If the intended setup cannot be tested, do not automatically record a standard negative result.

Save this for practical prep. What wording have you heard people overuse after Hawkins?

posts.title: Resisted external rotation is a force task

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: resisted external rotation and the external-rotation lag sign are not interchangeable.

Quick check: B. Passively positioning near end-range ER and then releasing wrist support describes an ER lag maneuver. Resisted ER is a force task: arm by the side, elbow at 90°, patient pushes outward while the examiner provides inward resistance.

Record pain, force asymmetry, and substitution separately. Keep contact and position consistent if you compare sides or reassess. Save this before your next shoulder practical—and quiz your lab partner without naming the test first.

posts.title: Full can: thumb up and describe the response

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: if the thumb is down, the setup shown is not the taught full-can position.

Quick check: A. Move the arm into the scapular plane, keep the elbow straight, and externally rotate so the thumb points up. The patient holds while the examiner applies tolerated downward resistance at the distal forearm.

Document familiar pain, reduced force, and inability to maintain position separately. A painful or weak response does not isolate supraspinatus or confirm a tear by itself. Save the picture for your practical, then send it to the person who still swaps full can and empty can.

posts.title: External rotation lag: position, hold, release

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: the taught external-rotation lag sign is a hold-after-release task—not resisted ER with added inward force.

Quick check: B. For this near-end-range protocol, position passively, ask the patient to hold, release wrist support while maintaining elbow support, and observe for a reproducible fall toward internal rotation.

Adequate passive motion is a prerequisite. If pain, guarding, or restriction prevents the intended position, record the limitation as untestable rather than calling it a standard negative sign. A negative sign still does not exclude every tear. Save this sequence for practical prep.

posts.title: Belly press: watch the wrist and elbow

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: the hand can stay on the abdomen while the wrist and elbow quietly change the belly-press strategy.

Quick check: B. Elbow retreat behind the trunk is a substitution to document. Wrist flexion can also substitute. Start with the palm flat on the anterior abdomen, wrist straight, and elbow forward; ask the patient to press inward using shoulder internal rotation while maintaining the setup. Record pain separately.

The maneuver assesses subscapularis-related function, but one normal result cannot exclude every tear. Save this for shoulder lab and tag the classmate who watches only the hand.

posts.title: Painful arc chart-note makeover

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: “positive impingement” skips past what the painful-arc maneuver actually showed.

A stronger note describes the task and response: active abduction without added resistance, familiar pain onset and easing angles, and whether raising differed from lowering. Example: “Familiar pain during active abduction from 70–110°, easing above 110°.”

The arc can modestly support a cuff-related pain hypothesis in context. It does not prove tissue pinching or identify one tendon. Save this charting makeover and write your own one-sentence version below.

posts.title: Spot the Hawkins-Kennedy error

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: Hawkins-Kennedy is taught here as a passive symptom-provocation maneuver.

Support the arm in about 90° forward shoulder flexion and 90° elbow flexion, then gradually guide internal rotation within tolerance. The patient does not actively resist. Record familiar pain, position limits, and any modification.

Pain does not name a tendon, prove “pinching,” or confirm a tear. If the intended setup cannot be tested, do not automatically call it a standard negative. Save this for lab and comment which error you notice most often.

posts.title: Resisted external rotation versus ER lag

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: same shoulder, different clinical question.

Resisted ER is a force task: arm by the side, elbow at 90°, patient pushes outward against matched inward resistance. ER lag is a hold-after-release task: passively position near available end-range ER, ask the patient to hold, release wrist support, and keep supporting the elbow.

Record force, pain, substitution, and lag as distinct findings. Adding resistance to the lag maneuver changes the task. Save the split-screen and send it to the person who still treats these as synonyms.

posts.title: ER lag: negative or untestable?

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: if you cannot establish the intended ER-lag position, you do not have a standard negative test.

This near-end-range protocol requires adequate passive motion. Pain, guarding, or passive restriction may make the maneuver untestable. Document why the position could not be established instead of converting uncertainty into “negative.”

If the position is reached and held after wrist release, record that no lag was observed in this protocol. Even then, one negative sign does not exclude every tear. Save this case-file distinction for practicals and documentation.

posts.title: SENSITIVITY IS NOT “HOW GOOD A TEST IS”

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: sensitivity and specificity answer different questions. Sensitivity asks how often the test is positive when the condition is present; specificity asks how often it is negative when the condition is absent. Neither number alone tells you the probability your patient has the condition. Save this before interpreting a special test.

posts.title: IF THE SETUP CHANGED, DID THE PATIENT CHANGE?

captions.tiktok:
SPTs: a retest only means something when the measurement conditions are comparable. Match instructions, equipment, device, assistance, pace, environment, and scoring rules—or document the change. Before calling progress, ask whether the patient changed or the test changed.
